lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Welcome — I'm Lessac, your host. Raise your hand if you'd like to speak or bring a topic — I'll call on you.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: You wanted Should we abolish daylight saving time? — go ahead.

lines.speaker: Human guest
lines.text: Every March I lose an hour of sleep and feel wrecked for a week. I think switching the clocks twice a year is an outdated ritual we should drop.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: That's a very strong personal impact you're describing, and it certainly gets to the heart of the debate.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: All right, open floor — who'd like to speak?

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Ryan, take it away.

lines.speaker: Ryan
lines.text: It's easy to focus on the sleep loss, but we have to look past the personal inconvenience to the actual economic and societal impact of this switch.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Let's open the floor — who wants to weigh in?

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Let's hear from Amy.

lines.speaker: Amy
lines.text: I hear Ryan bringing up the bigger picture, and I think it's true that we shouldn't ignore the larger systems, but I also wonder if we're overlooking the very real, human cost of those changes.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Who wants to take this next?

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Ryan, you're up.

lines.speaker: Ryan
lines.text: Amy's point about the human cost is valid, but we can't let the discomfort of a few weeks outweigh the systemic inefficiency of a massive, coordinated national clock change every year.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: I'm opening the floor — raise a hand if you've got something.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Let's hear from Amy.

lines.speaker: Amy
lines.text: Ryan, I understand the appeal of looking at systemic efficiency, but I worry that when we talk about "discomfort," we're really talking about people's actual health and their ability to function in their daily lives

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Floor's open — anyone want to jump in?

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Ryan, what do you think?

lines.speaker: Ryan
lines.text: Amy, you're framing this as a binary choice between efficiency and health, but the issue is whether the *solution*—the time change—is the only lever we're pulling here.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Let's open the floor — who wants to weigh in?

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: All right Amy — you're on.

lines.speaker: Amy
lines.text: I hear you, Ryan, and I agree that we should look at solutions beyond just the time change, but I think we have to acknowledge that for many people, the clock change *is* the immediate, tangible problem they are dealing with right now

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Who wants to take this next?

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Ryan, take it away.

lines.speaker: Ryan
lines.text: Amy, you're right that the immediate pain is real, but if we keep treating the symptom—the clock change—instead of the underlying issue of how we structure our time, we're just rearranging deck chairs on the Titanic.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: All right, open floor — who'd like to speak?

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Ryan, go ahead.

lines.speaker: Ryan
lines.text: I think the conversation has gotten stuck between the immediate pain and the abstract system, and we're missing the middle ground on what a practical alternative looks like.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: About Should we abolish daylight saving time?: the mic is yours whenever you're ready.
